title: Causal structure, asymptotics and singularities
scope: Global, whole-spacetime methods for arbitrary Lorentzian spacetimes. Causal curves, time orientation, causal and chronological futures and pasts, closed timelike curves and spacetime topology; time functions, domains of dependence, Cauchy surfaces and horizons, global hyperbolicity and existence of maximal curves. Conformal compactification and Penrose diagrams as a technique, with Minkowski space as the model, plus conformal infinity (i+, i-, i0, null infinity) and asymptotic flatness. Horizons as causal boundaries in general, trapped and marginally trapped surfaces. Geodesic congruences with expansion, shear and rotation, the timelike and null Raychaudhuri equations, convergence conditions, focusing and caustics. Singularities as geodesic incompleteness and inextendibility, curvature, spacelike, timelike and naked singularities and their classification (including BKL), the Penrose, Hawking and Hawking-Penrose singularity theorems, cosmic censorship, and exotic causal geometries (traversable wormholes, warp drives). Diagrams and horizons of named spacetimes, energy-condition definitions, the Cauchy problem and asymptotic mass definitions live in their own domains.

concepts.title: Global causal structure of spacetime
aliases: causal structure of a curved spacetime
concepts.summary: In a curved spacetime the metric fixes a light cone at every event, and the pattern of these cones, together with a choice of future, decides which events can influence which across the whole manifold. Global methods study this pattern and properties of the manifold as a whole, rather than tensor equations at a point, and they are the tools behind horizons, Cauchy surfaces and singularity theorems.
concepts.notes: Two metrics with the same null cones at every event share the same causal relations, which is why conformal methods (conformal-invariance, owned by manifolds-and-metrics) preserve causal structure. The flat-space version (absolute past, future, elsewhere) is owned by special-relativity.

concepts.title: Time orientability
aliases: future and past sheets of the light cone
concepts.summary: A time orientation is a choice of which half of each light cone counts as the future; a spacetime is time-orientable if that choice can be made continuously over the whole manifold. Then every timelike or null vector is consistently future- or past-pointing, which is needed before causal futures and pasts make sense globally.
concepts.notes: In Minkowski space a vector X is future-pointing when its inner product with a fixed future timelike reference vector has the appropriate sign (DIV ch08). GA ch19 contrasts a strip of cones glued into a cylinder with and without a flip of future and past, and suggests entropy increase as a practical way to pick the future.

concepts.title: Causal curve
concepts.summary: A causal curve is a curve whose tangent is everywhere timelike or null and future-pointing, the possible history of a signal or particle. It is inextendible when it has no endpoint in the spacetime in either direction, the notion used to define Cauchy surfaces and domains of dependence.
concepts.notes: Timelike curves as particle histories are owned by special-relativity; this concept adds future direction and inextendibility for global arguments.

concepts.title: Causal and chronological future and past
aliases: causal regions of a world line
concepts.summary: The causal future J+(p) of an event is every event reachable from p along a future causal curve, and the causal past J-(p) is every event from which p can be reached; the chronological versions I+ and I- use timelike curves only and sit inside J+ and J-. These sets, taken for events, world lines or whole regions, are the building blocks of horizons and domains of dependence.

names: causal regions of a world line

merged_from: causal regions of a world line
concepts.notes: GA ch19 splits spacetime relative to a whole world line into regions that can be seen and influenced, only influenced, only seen, or neither; seeing and influencing are bounded by different horizons.

concepts.title: Closed timelike curve
concepts.summary: A closed timelike curve is a future-directed timelike world line that returns to an event it already passed through, so an observer always moving into their local future meets their own past. Such curves violate causality and are generally regarded as unphysical, yet exact solutions contain them, for instance near the ring singularity of Kerr and in anti-de Sitter space before unwrapping its time.
concepts.notes: Kerr examples: on the negative-r side the axial direction becomes timelike, so circles of constant t, r, theta are timelike (DIV ch20, GA ch29). AdS example: global time runs around a circle on the hyperboloid (GA ch49). Excluding such curves is the chronology condition used in the Hawking-Penrose theorem.

concepts.title: Topology of spacetime
concepts.summary: The topology of a spacetime is the set of its properties that survive continuous deformation: whether spatial sections are closed, how regions are glued together, whether there are handles. The field equations are local and do not fix it, so spacetimes with identical local geometry can differ globally.
concepts.notes: Example: the Einstein static universe has topology of a line times a 3-sphere, drawn as a cylinder (GA ch19). The general local-versus-global distinction is owned by manifolds-and-metrics.

concepts.title: Time function
concepts.summary: A time function is a scalar field on spacetime whose gradient is everywhere timelike, so it increases along every future causal curve and its level sets are spacelike slices. Its existence rules out closed timelike curves and gives a global notion of successive moments.

concepts.title: Domain of dependence
aliases: future and past domain of dependence
concepts.summary: The future domain of dependence of a set S is the set of events every past-inextendible causal curve through which must cross S, and similarly for the past; together they form the region whose physics is completely fixed by data on S. In 1+1 Minkowski space the future domain of an interval is the triangle rising above it at 45 degrees.
concepts.notes: Removing a point from spacetime shrinks domains of dependence, a legacy exercise showing global notions are sensitive to holes.

concepts.title: Cauchy surface
concepts.summary: A Cauchy surface is a spacelike (more generally achronal) hypersurface met exactly once by every inextendible causal curve, so its domain of dependence is the whole spacetime and data on it determine everything. Not every spacelike slice is Cauchy: an achronal surface can miss curves that escape past its edge.
concepts.notes: Its role as the carrier of initial data in the Cauchy problem is owned by einstein-field-equations.

concepts.title: Global hyperbolicity
concepts.summary: A spacetime is globally hyperbolic if it possesses a Cauchy surface. Such spacetimes are the arena for deterministic evolution: wave equations have unique global solutions, the manifold splits as a line of time times a 3-manifold, and any two causally related events are joined by a longest causal curve.
concepts.notes: The name echoes hyperbolic wave equations. The product-splitting statement is Geroch's theorem.

concepts.title: Cauchy horizon
aliases: boundary of the domain of dependence
concepts.summary: A Cauchy horizon is the null boundary of the domain of dependence of a surface, beyond which the future is no longer fixed by the data on that surface. It differs from an event horizon: it marks the end of predictability rather than the end of escape to infinity.
concepts.notes: The inner horizon of Reissner-Nordstrom and Kerr black holes is the standard example and is owned by black-holes; its blueshift instability motivates strong cosmic censorship.

concepts.title: Maximal globally hyperbolic development
concepts.summary: For vacuum initial data on a slice, there is a unique (up to isometry) largest globally hyperbolic spacetime in which that slice is a Cauchy surface carrying the data, and every other such development embeds into it. It is the global counterpart of local existence and uniqueness for the Einstein equations.
concepts.notes: Whether this development can be extended beyond its Cauchy horizon is exactly the question posed by strong cosmic censorship.

concepts.title: Existence of maximal causal curves (Avez-Seifert theorem)
aliases: existence of a maximal timelike curve
compactness of the space of causal curves
concepts.summary: In a globally hyperbolic spacetime any event in the domain of dependence of a Cauchy surface is joined to that surface by a causal curve of greatest proper time, and that curve is a timelike geodesic meeting the surface orthogonally with no focal point in between. The technical input is that the space of causal curves between them is compact, so proper time attains its maximum.

names: existence of a maximal timelike curve
compactness of the space of causal curves

merged_from: existence of a maximal timelike curve
compactness of the space of causal curves
concepts.notes: GA presents it as a plausibility argument with a margin note on compactness ("no curves escape to infinity"); it is one horn of the contradiction in the cosmological singularity theorem.

concepts.title: Asymptotic flatness
concepts.summary: A spacetime is asymptotically flat if, far from an isolated source, its metric approaches the Minkowski metric (with specified fall-off of the corrections) so curvature vanishes at large distance. This boundary condition fixes integration constants in solutions, lets distant observers and total mass be defined, and is the setting for event horizons and outgoing radiation.
concepts.notes: Uses across books: fixing Phi and Lambda to zero at infinity in static spherical stars (SCH ch10, GA ch21), the Schwarzschild and Kerr limits, h_ab -> 0 in linearized theory (DIV ch21), and fall-off along outgoing null rays for Bondi analysis (DIV ch23). Penrose's asymptotically simple spacetimes (DIV ch18) make it precise via a conformal compactification with a Minkowski-like null boundary. DIV ch13 notes the condition alone cannot rule out flat space as a solution.

concepts.title: Conformal compactification
aliases: conformal mapping onto the Einstein static universe
concepts.summary: Conformal compactification brings infinity to a finite place: choose coordinates (often arctan of null coordinates) with finite range, then multiply the physical metric by a conformal factor that vanishes at infinity, giving an unphysical metric that is regular on the added boundary. Because conformal rescaling preserves light cones, the compactified picture shows the true causal structure while distorting distances.
concepts.notes: The arctan map sends the whole real line to (-pi/2, pi/2) and is applied to each null coordinate separately. GA ch19 first tries V = 1/v and finds the rescaled line element well behaved. DIV ch25 and GA ch49 apply the method to Robertson-Walker, de Sitter and anti-de Sitter by identifying the rescaled metric with the Einstein static universe.

concepts.title: Penrose diagram
concepts.summary: A Penrose diagram is a two-dimensional picture of a conformally compactified spacetime, with angular directions suppressed, in which radial light rays run at 45 degrees and the entire spacetime, including its infinities and singularities, fits in a finite figure. Distances are distorted but which events can signal which can be read off by eye.
concepts.notes: Diagrams of named spacetimes belong to their domains: Kruskal, Reissner-Nordstrom, Kerr and collapse to black-holes; Robertson-Walker to cosmological-kinematics; de Sitter to cosmological-dynamics. GA ch41 uses the diagram to show how inflation lowers the big-bang line.

concepts.title: Penrose diagram of Minkowski spacetime
concepts.summary: Compactifying flat spacetime with arctan null coordinates maps it onto a bounded diamond (a triangle when only r >= 0 is drawn) inside the Einstein static cylinder. Its vertices are future and past timelike infinity and spatial infinity, its null edges are future and past null infinity, and it is the template for reading every other Penrose diagram.
concepts.notes: In DIV the image is |t' +- r'| < pi on the Einstein static universe. GA Example 19.2 shows every Minkowski world line starts at i-, so an observer eventually sees all particles: no particle or event horizon.

concepts.title: Conformal infinity
concepts.summary: Conformal infinity is the boundary added to a spacetime by conformal compactification, split according to which kind of curve ends there: timelike curves at i+ and i-, light rays on the null infinities, spacelike curves at spatial infinity. Its causal character is informative: null in Minkowski space, spacelike in de Sitter (which is why de Sitter observers have horizons), timelike in anti-de Sitter (which behaves like a box light can reach).
concepts.notes: Caution from DIV ch25: its Robertson-Walker diagrams put scri labels on the big bang and crunch, which are singular edges rather than infinity. The AdS boundary is itself a flat spacetime of one lower dimension; its holographic role is owned by quantum-gravity-and-beyond.

concepts.title: Future and past null infinity
concepts.summary: Future null infinity is the boundary where outgoing light rays end as their affine parameter grows without bound, and past null infinity is where incoming rays begin. In an asymptotically flat spacetime these are null surfaces, the place where outgoing radiation is read off and the reference for defining an event horizon.
concepts.notes: Bondi mass, news and peeling at null infinity are owned by gravitational-waves.

concepts.title: Future and past timelike infinity
concepts.summary: Future timelike infinity i+ is the idealised endpoint of timelike curves as proper time runs to plus infinity, and past timelike infinity i- is their idealised origin. In the Minkowski Penrose diagram each is a single vertex, the top and bottom corners.

concepts.title: Spatial infinity
concepts.summary: Spatial infinity i0 is the limit reached by going to infinite distance along spacelike curves at finite time; in compactified Minkowski space all constant-time slices end at this single point. It is causally disconnected from every observer.
concepts.notes: DIV ch18 notes it looks like a circle when a spatial dimension is restored but is regarded as one point. ADM mass is defined there (einstein-field-equations).

concepts.title: Observer-dependent horizon
concepts.summary: A horizon is the boundary of the causal past (or future) of an observer's world line: the edge of the region that observer can ever see (or influence). For accelerated observers and in cosmology this boundary depends on the chosen world line and a different observer has a different one, unlike the absolute event horizon of a black hole defined relative to all of future null infinity.
concepts.notes: Example: the Rindler horizon of a uniformly accelerating observer (special-relativity). Cosmological particle and event horizons are owned by cosmological-kinematics; black-hole event horizons by black-holes.

concepts.title: Trapped surface
concepts.summary: A closed trapped surface is a compact spacelike 2-surface for which both families of future-directed light rays leaving it orthogonally, outgoing and ingoing, converge, so both wavefronts have less area than the surface. Every round sphere inside the Schwarzschild radius is trapped; the existence of such a surface is the input of Penrose's singularity theorem.
concepts.notes: Construction (GA ch26, DIV ch18): flash light from every point of a sphere and compare the areas of the inner and outer envelopes. Instances: Kruskal region II, Reissner-Nordstrom and Kerr regions II. Legacy warns against the myth that light "slows down"; trapping is a statement about null expansions.

concepts.title: Apparent horizon
concepts.summary: An apparent horizon is the outer boundary of trapped surfaces on a given time slice, made of marginally trapped 2-surfaces whose outgoing light rays momentarily neither expand nor contract. Unlike the event horizon it can be located from data on one slice without knowing the future, depends on the slicing, and lies inside or on the event horizon.
concepts.notes: Schutz offers it as the practical horizon for numerical relativity after showing that the event horizon is teleological.

concepts.title: Geodesic congruence
concepts.summary: A geodesic congruence is a family of geodesics filling a region with exactly one through each event, so its tangents form a smooth velocity field; a cloud of freely falling dust is the physical picture. Studying how neighbouring members spread, shear and twist is the starting point for focusing arguments.
concepts.notes: DIV ch10 uses a one-parameter family sweeping a 2-surface to derive geodesic deviation; DIV ch24 uses a non-crossing congruence in Weyl's postulate.

concepts.title: Expansion (convergence) of a congruence
concepts.summary: The expansion theta of a timelike congruence is the divergence of its unit tangent field and equals the fractional rate of change of the volume of a small comoving blob per unit proper time; GA uses its negative, the convergence c. Negative expansion means neighbouring world lines are drawing together.

names: convergence of comoving Friedmann world lines
theta as d ln V / d tau

merged_from: convergence of comoving Friedmann world lines
concepts.notes: Example (GA ch50): comoving dust in a Friedmann model has convergence -3H, so an expanding universe has positive convergence toward the past.

concepts.title: Expansion, shear and rotation decomposition
concepts.summary: The velocity gradient of a timelike geodesic congruence, projected orthogonal to the flow, splits into a trace (expansion: isotropic change of volume), a symmetric trace-free part (shear: change of shape at fixed volume) and an antisymmetric part (rotation: twisting of neighbouring world lines). Acting on a connecting vector it gives how that separation changes along the flow.

names: trace and trace-free decomposition of the velocity gradient
decomposition B = theta h/3 + sigma + omega

merged_from: trace and trace-free decomposition of the velocity gradient
concepts.notes: GA ch50 uses only the trace/trace-free split in the main text (rotation vanishes for its gradient field) and gives the full decomposition in Exercise 50.2. The null analogue (optical scalars) is owned by gravitational-waves.

concepts.title: Hypersurface-orthogonal geodesic congruence
aliases: zero rotation of a hypersurface-orthogonal congruence
concepts.summary: Launching timelike geodesics orthogonally from a spacelike hypersurface and labelling events by proper time along them gives a scalar whose gradient is the congruence's unit tangent. Such a gradient flow stays orthogonal to the level surfaces and has zero rotation, removing the only term in the Raychaudhuri equation that resists focusing.

names: zero rotation of a hypersurface-orthogonal congruence

merged_from: zero rotation of a hypersurface-orthogonal congruence
concepts.notes: The cosmological substratum being orthogonal to homogeneous slices is an application owned by cosmological-kinematics.

concepts.title: Raychaudhuri equation
aliases: volume evolution from the Ricci tensor
concepts.summary: Along a timelike geodesic congruence the expansion obeys d theta/d tau = -theta^2/3 - sigma^2 + omega^2 - R_ab u^a u^b. Expansion itself, shear, and positive Ricci curvature along the flow all drive convergence, while only rotation opposes it; this is the precise sense in which gravity attracts.

names: volume evolution from the Ricci tensor

merged_from: volume evolution from the Ricci tensor
concepts.notes: Precursor (GA ch35): a small ball of particles initially at rest relative to its centre has second volume derivative equal to minus R_ab u^a u^b times the volume, negative for ordinary matter; in vacuum the volume does not accelerate even as its shape distorts. Legacy explains the plus sign of vorticity and adds a divergence-of-acceleration term for non-geodesic flows; Weyl curvature acts only through shear.

concepts.title: Timelike convergence condition
concepts.summary: The timelike convergence condition requires R_ab V^a V^b >= 0 for every timelike (or causal) vector, so the Ricci term in the Raychaudhuri equation always helps focusing. Through the Einstein equations with zero cosmological constant it is equivalent to the strong energy condition on matter.

names: SEC implies timelike convergence only for Lambda = 0

concepts.notes: A positive cosmological constant violates it, so Lambda can defeat timelike focusing (legacy chapter 22).

concepts.title: Focusing theorem
concepts.summary: For a hypersurface-orthogonal timelike geodesic congruence obeying the timelike convergence condition, the Raychaudhuri equation gives d theta/d tau <= -theta^2/3. So a congruence that is converging somewhere, theta_0 < 0, must reach infinite convergence (a focal point) within proper time 3/|theta_0|, provided the geodesics extend that far.

names: trace inequality for the velocity gradient
time reversal of the focusing argument

merged_from: trace inequality for the velocity gradient
time reversal of the focusing argument
concepts.notes: The inequality comes from dropping the non-negative shear square (the trace inequality: the contracted square of the velocity gradient is at least theta^2/3). Integrating is like the blow-up of dy/dx = y^2. Reversing time turns an expanding universe into a past-converging congruence, which is how the argument bounds the past.

concepts.title: Caustic
concepts.summary: A caustic is where neighbouring rays or geodesics of a congruence cross, so the congruence description (and any coordinates built from it) breaks down while spacetime itself stays perfectly regular. Focusing to a caustic is therefore not yet a singularity; even straight lines in flat spacetime cross and continue.

names: focusing is not yet a singularity

concepts.notes: Example (DIV ch22): colliding plane waves focus each other's null generators; Rosen-type coordinates degenerate on fold surfaces with finite curvature, while the true curvature singularity forms later. This gap is why singularity theorems need global hypotheses.

concepts.title: Null geodesic congruence
concepts.summary: A null geodesic congruence is a family of light rays filling a region, one through each event, with affinely parametrized tangent l. Its expansion measures the fractional rate at which the cross-sectional area of a thin beam grows per unit affine parameter; the signs of the outgoing and ingoing expansions of a 2-surface decide whether it is trapped.
concepts.notes: Legacy computes the outgoing null expansion of Schwarzschild spheres as proportional to 1 - 2m/r, negative inside the horizon. Shear and twist of null congruences (optical scalars) are owned by gravitational-waves; a null congruence needs a 2-dimensional screen space orthogonal to l and a second null vector.

concepts.title: Null Raychaudhuri equation
concepts.summary: Along an affinely parametrized null geodesic congruence the expansion obeys d theta/d lambda = -theta^2/2 - sigma^2 + omega^2 - R_ab l^a l^b. With the null convergence condition and zero twist, light beams that start converging must focus in finite affine parameter, the engine of Penrose's theorem.
concepts.notes: DIV writes it for the complex combination of expansion and twist. The cosmological constant drops out of R_ab l^a l^b, so null focusing survives Lambda (legacy). An affine parameter is essential.

concepts.title: Null convergence condition
concepts.summary: The null convergence condition requires R_ab k^a k^b >= 0 for every null vector k, guaranteeing that light-ray congruences are focused rather than defocused by curvature. Via the Einstein equations it follows from the null energy condition, is implied by the weak energy condition, and is unaffected by a cosmological constant.

concepts.title: Ricci focusing versus Weyl shear
aliases: Ricci focusing versus Weyl shear of light bundles
concepts.summary: A thin bundle of light passing through matter, where R_ab k^a k^b is positive, is focused isotropically like a converging lens, enlarging a round image. Weyl curvature instead acts like an astigmatic lens, squeezing one transverse direction and stretching the other, so circles become ellipses without net area focusing at first order.

names: Ricci focusing versus Weyl shear of light bundles
volume and shape ask different questions

merged_from: Ricci focusing versus Weyl shear of light bundles
concepts.notes: GA illustrates with Penrose's transparent Sun: stars seen through it look enlarged and round, stars seen past its rim look elliptical.

concepts.title: Generic condition
concepts.summary: The generic condition requires every causal geodesic to meet, somewhere along it, curvature with a non-zero tidal component transverse to its direction. It fails only in special, highly symmetric spacetimes and ensures focusing actually occurs, which is why it appears as a hypothesis of the Hawking-Penrose theorem.

concepts.title: Geodesic incompleteness
concepts.summary: A spacetime is geodesically complete if every geodesic can be extended to arbitrary values of its affine parameter in both directions. If some timelike or null geodesic ends after finite proper time or affine parameter and the spacetime cannot be extended to continue it, the spacetime is incomplete, which is the standard modern definition of a singular spacetime.

names: geodesic incompleteness of the steady-state model

merged_from: geodesic incompleteness of the steady-state model
concepts.notes: Incompleteness alone may just signal an unextended chart (GA Example 26.2), or a deleted point, so it must be paired with inextendibility. Example: the steady-state (flat de Sitter) patch is past null incomplete though comoving observers live forever (DIV ch25). Minkowski is complete; Kruskal is maximal but incomplete.

concepts.title: Extension of a spacetime
concepts.summary: An extension embeds a spacetime as a proper part of a larger smooth spacetime into which its incomplete geodesics continue, usually by letting coordinates take values the old chart could not reach. A maximal (inextendible) spacetime admits none, so every geodesic either runs forever or ends at a genuine singularity.
concepts.notes: Examples: the Rindler wedge extends to all of Minkowski space by letting U and V range over the reals (GA Example 26.3); matter-filled Robertson-Walker models are inextendible (DIV ch25). Complete spacetimes are maximal but not conversely. Maximal analytic extensions of Schwarzschild, RN and Kerr are owned by black-holes.

concepts.title: Spacetime singularity
aliases: singularity as breakdown of the manifold structure
concepts.summary: A spacetime singularity is not a point of spacetime but an edge where the smooth Lorentzian manifold description fails: observers or light rays reach it in finite proper time or affine parameter and cannot continue, and typically curvature grows without bound. Known physics makes no prediction there; unlike infinity, a singularity lies a finite proper time away.

names: singularity as breakdown of the manifold structure

merged_from: singularity as breakdown of the manifold structure
concepts.notes: GA ch26 illustrates with the tip of a cone, where no small patch looks flat. In conformal diagrams both singularities and infinities are boundaries; the distinction is finite versus infinite proper distance (GA ch19).

concepts.title: Curvature singularity
concepts.summary: A curvature singularity is where scalar invariants built from the Riemann tensor, such as the Kretschmann scalar, diverge along curves reaching it in finite affine parameter, so tidal forces become unbounded and no change of coordinates can make the geometry regular. It contrasts with a coordinate singularity, which is an artefact of a bad chart.
concepts.notes: Examples: r = 0 of Schwarzschild, where tides scale as M/r^3 (SCH ch11, GA ch25, DIV ch17); r = 0 of Reissner-Nordstrom (DIV ch19); the end of region IV of the Penrose-Khan colliding-wave solution (DIV ch22). GA ch16 contrasts it with a Newtonian singularity where only density diverges. The r = 2M coordinate singularity is owned by black-holes.

concepts.title: Spacelike singularity
aliases: spacelike singularity as boundary of spacetime
concepts.summary: A spacelike singularity is a singular boundary lying at a moment rather than a place: it is to the future (or past) of every nearby event, so once inside the region it bounds it cannot be avoided, and in a Penrose diagram it is a horizontal edge. The Schwarzschild r = 0 and the big bang are the standard examples.

names: spacelike singularity as boundary of spacetime

merged_from: spacelike singularity as boundary of spacetime
concepts.notes: Inside the Schwarzschild horizon r is a time coordinate, which is why r = 0 is spacelike there. In Robertson-Walker diagrams every world line starts on the singularity; in Kruskal only those entering region II end on it.

concepts.title: Timelike singularity
concepts.summary: A timelike singularity has a timelike locus, a place beside observers in space rather than a moment in their future, drawn as a vertical line in a Penrose diagram. Future-directed world lines are not forced into it and can steer around it, as near r = 0 inside the inner horizon of charged and rotating black holes.
concepts.notes: Reissner-Nordstrom r = 0 is also repulsive: the charge term turns timelike geodesics around before they reach it (GA ch29). A timelike singularity threatens predictability because it can send signals into its future.

concepts.title: Classification of spacetime singularities
aliases: scalar versus parallelly propagated curvature singularity
concepts.summary: Singularities are classified by how curvature misbehaves along incomplete curves: scalar curvature singularities where invariants diverge, weaker non-scalar (whimper-type) ones where curvature is unbounded only in a parallelly propagated frame, and quasi-regular ones with bounded curvature. Anisotropic cosmological singularities are further described by their shape, a region collapsing to a line (cigar) or a sheet (pancake).
concepts.notes: Cigar and pancake behaviour is shown for Kasner and matter-filled Bianchi models (DIV ch24); whimper singularities occur only in special Bianchi models.

concepts.title: BKL singularity
concepts.summary: The Belinski-Khalatnikov-Lifshitz analysis suggests that a generic cosmological singularity is locally a chaotic sequence of Kasner-like epochs, each point contracting and expanding along different axes, far more complex than the isotropic Friedmann big bang. It motivates studying anisotropic models and remains a research topic.

concepts.title: Naked singularity
concepts.summary: A naked singularity is one not hidden behind an event horizon, so causal signals from it can reach distant observers and influence the exterior. Super-extremal Reissner-Nordstrom (charge exceeding mass) and Kerr (spin exceeding mass) contain them, which would destroy predictability if such spacetimes formed.
concepts.notes: GA ch27 calls the past (white-hole) singularity of Kruskal naked because it can send light into region I. DIV ch20 draws light spiralling out of a super-extremal Kerr ring. The super-extremal cases themselves are owned by black-holes.

concepts.title: Cosmic censorship
concepts.summary: Cosmic censorship is Penrose's conjecture that physically reasonable evolution does not produce naked singularities. The weak form says singularities arising from regular asymptotically flat data stay hidden behind event horizons; the strong form says generic data have a maximal globally hyperbolic development that cannot be extended past a Cauchy horizon, so determinism survives.
concepts.notes: Unproven, with several inequivalent formulations; Schutz notes counterexamples to one form involving weak null singularities and that the big bang is an unavoidable naked singularity.

concepts.title: Singularity theorems
concepts.summary: Singularity theorems show that a spacetime satisfying an initial or boundary condition (a trapped surface or everywhere-converging slice), a curvature condition (an energy condition via Einstein's equations) and a causality condition must contain incomplete causal geodesics. They prove something singular happens without symmetry assumptions but say nothing about where it is or whether curvature blows up.

names: singularity theorems need extra global hypotheses

concepts.notes: DIV ch20 organises them as a three-ingredient template following Senovilla. They answer the objection that collapse and big-bang singularities are artefacts of symmetry (DIV ch17, ch26; SCH ch13). The logic: focusing forces conjugate points, but global hyperbolicity guarantees maximal geodesics without them, a contradiction unless geodesics end.

concepts.title: Hawking cosmological singularity theorem
aliases: proof by contradiction via maximal curves
concepts.summary: If spacetime is globally hyperbolic, obeys the strong energy condition, and the future normals to a Cauchy surface converge everywhere at rate at least c_0 > 0, then no future timelike curve from that surface lasts longer than 3/c_0 in proper time. Run backwards for an expanding universe, every past-directed world line has finite length: a beginning without assuming homogeneity.

names: proof by contradiction via maximal curves
singularity theorems for a universe like ours

merged_from: proof by contradiction via maximal curves
concepts.notes: Proof (GA ch50): a maximal curve to any event exists and must be a normal geodesic without focal points, but focusing forces a focal point by 3/c_0, so no event lies farther away. The explicit a = 0 singularity of Friedmann models is owned by cosmological-dynamics.

concepts.title: Penrose singularity theorem
concepts.summary: Penrose's 1965 theorem: a spacetime with a non-compact Cauchy surface, obeying the null convergence (null energy) condition and containing a closed trapped surface, has at least one incomplete null geodesic. It shows gravitational collapse leads to something singular without spherical symmetry, and underlies trapped surfaces lying inside event horizons.
concepts.notes: Cited in connection with Penrose's 2020 Nobel Prize (SCH ch11, DIV ch01). Legacy stresses what it does not give: the location of the singularity or a curvature blow-up.

concepts.title: Hawking-Penrose singularity theorem
concepts.summary: The 1970 Hawking-Penrose theorem states that a spacetime with no closed timelike curves, satisfying the timelike and null convergence conditions and the generic condition, and containing a closed trapped surface (or an analogous converging condition), is causal-geodesically incomplete. It combines timelike and null focusing in one result.
concepts.notes: DIV ch20 uses it to fill each slot of the general three-ingredient template.

concepts.title: Traversable wormhole
concepts.summary: A traversable wormhole is a hypothetical tunnel geometry that travellers could actually pass through, possibly linking distant regions or universes. Unlike the Einstein-Rosen bridge, which pinches off too fast, known traversable constructions need matter of negative energy density, violating the standard energy conditions.
concepts.notes: Wormholes with non-trivial topology can also create closed timelike curves, which ties them to causality violation.

concepts.title: Alcubierre warp drive
concepts.summary: The Alcubierre metric describes a bubble of distorted spacetime moving along a path: inside it light cones are shifted by the bubble velocity, so the bubble can outrun light as judged from far away while nothing ever leaves its local light cone. Building it requires negative energy density.
concepts.notes: GA Example 5.4 sets ds^2 = 0 to find dx/dt = v_s f +- 1 and shows the cones tipping inside the bubble. It is a good exercise in distinguishing local from global speed limits.
